passage: Sagar kept a magazine picture of the game console folded in his pocket: two thousand rupees. Dad had already said it was too much this month. Sagar could sulk, but he sat on the roof steps in Kathmandu and made himself think. If I insist, I may get nothing. A cheaper one still plays games. Or I wait until my birthday in two months, and Dad might say yes then. That night he said, "Dad, could I have the smaller console, or wait till my birthday and put my own savings towards it?" Dad rubbed his chin. "That I can think about." Sagar decided that half a loaf was better than none.

qa.q: How much did the console in Sagar's picture cost?
qa.a: The console cost two thousand rupees.

qa.q: What was Sagar feeling as he sat on the roof steps, and what did he decide to do about it?
qa.a: He felt disappointed and tempted to sulk, but he chose to think through his options instead.

qa.q: What else could Sagar do to make a compromise more likely?
qa.a: He could offer his own savings or take on extra chores, because it shows effort and lowers what Dad has to pay.

qa.q: How might Dad feel hearing two options instead of a flat demand?
qa.a: Probably relieved and more willing to talk, since he said he could think about it.

grounding: A boy wanting an expensive console accepts that a cheaper one or waiting for his birthday is better than nothing.

subtopic: A power cut or rain spoils plans
subtype: Approach: switching to an indoor activity [Revision]
passage: Saturday night. Rain! It came at ten, just as we were leaving for the ground. Samir's cousin and I stood at the window for five minutes looking sad. Then Samir said, "What if today is a carrom day?" So it was. Three of us on the floor around the board, and after lunch Nani's ludo box came out, and the fight over the yellow tokens was louder than any cricket match. I lost three games and won one. Pakoras at four while the rain drummed on the tin roof. Cricket next week. Honestly, this felt like a different kind of good day, not a wasted one. Aditi

qa.q: What games did the children play after the rain started?
qa.a: They played carrom on the floor and later ludo.

qa.q: How did Aditi feel by the end of the day?
qa.a: Content, since Aditi calls it a different kind of good day and not a wasted one. 😊

qa.q: What other approach could turn a rained-off day into something good, and why?
qa.a: They could cook something together, like pakoras, or plan the match for next week, because a shared activity keeps spirits up.

qa.q: How might Samir's idea of a carrom day have felt to the others at the window?
qa.a: Probably like a relief, since they were looking sad and Samir gave them something to do straight away.

grounding: Aditi and the others, after rain cancels cricket, switch to indoor games and count it as a different fun day.

subtopic: A power cut or rain spoils plans
subtype: Approach: thinking of what is still possible [Thinking]
passage: Nirmala's tablet screen blinked off when the whole village went dark at eight. She wanted to shout. Instead she stood still in the courtyard and counted. No videos, no game. But: I can read my story book by the candle. I can ask Dadi for the tale of the clever crow. We can play antakshari, because songs need no light. She set the candle on a steel plate, away from the blankets, and carried it in. By the time her neighbour Farida came over with a lantern, the whole family was singing on the charpai, and Nirmala had forgotten about the tablet.

qa.q: Which game did Nirmala think of playing in the dark?
qa.a: Nirmala thought of playing antakshari.

qa.q: How did Nirmala feel when the tablet went dark, and what did she do with that feeling?
qa.a: She felt frustrated and wanted to shout, but she stood still and thought about what she could still do.

qa.q: What safer light could Nirmala use if the power cut lasts long, and why?
qa.a: A torch, because unlike a candle it cannot tip over near blankets or small children.

qa.q: How might Dadi feel about being asked for the crow story?
qa.a: Probably pleased and warmed to be asked, since the whole family ended up gathered around singing and listening.

grounding: A girl in a night power cut lists what is still possible: reading by candle, a story from Dadi and antakshari.

subtopic: A power cut or rain spoils plans
passage: The colony picnic at the park had been rained off, so the families gathered in the community hall instead. Harsha's father, Omkar, spread a mat, his mother unpacked sandwiches, and a board game came out of a bag. Harsha dragged a chair to the wall and folded his arms. "Everything is spoiled," he said. His little sister held up the dice. "No." Around the mat, the games got louder and someone started a song. Harsha watched from his chair, chewing a cold sandwich, hearing every laugh. When it was time to go home, he realised he had spent the whole cosy afternoon looking at it from across the room.

qa.q: Where did the families gather after the picnic was rained off?
qa.a: The families gathered in the community hall.

qa.q: What was Harsha feeling as he sat by the wall, and how does his behaviour show it?
qa.a: Angry and disappointed, since he folded his arms, said everything was spoiled and refused the game.

qa.q: What could Harsha have done instead of sulking, and why?
qa.a: He could have joined the board game and treated it as a different kind of picnic, because the day was still there to enjoy.

qa.q: How might Harsha's father feel seeing him sit apart?
qa.a: Probably sad and a little helpless, since Omkar had spread the mat to make the day cosy and Harsha would not join.

grounding: A boy whose picnic is rained off sulks and blames, and misses the cosy day the family arranged.

subtopic: A power cut or rain spoils plans
subtype: Approach: preparing a torch and candles in advance [Action]
passage: The fan stopped mid-turn and the room went black. "Power cut again!" Jeevan groaned from the sofa. "Where is the torch?" "Second shelf, left side, behind the biscuit tin," Rafiq said, already moving. A click, and a white circle of light wobbled on the wall. "Matches?" "Same shelf, in the little steel box. I will hand it to you, Papa, and you light the candle." "Good boy. And the hand fan?" "On the hook by the door." Rafiq waved it at his father's face. "It happens every summer, so I keep everything in one place." Jeevan laughed. "Ten minutes and we are already comfortable. Thank you, Rafiq."

qa.q: Where did Rafiq keep the torch?
qa.a: He kept the torch on the second shelf, left side, behind the biscuit tin.

qa.q: How does Rafiq feel about helping when the lights go out?
qa.a: Calm and a little proud, since he already knew where each thing was and looked after his father's comfort.

qa.q: What else could Rafiq prepare for the next power cut, and why?
qa.a: He could keep spare batteries beside the torch, because a torch is only useful if it works when the lights go.

qa.q: How might Jeevan feel about the way the family handled the power cut?
qa.a: Relieved and grateful, since he laughed and thanked Rafiq after ten minutes, already comfortable. 🙂

grounding: A child keeps a torch, matches and a hand fan in a known place so he can help quickly in a summer power cut.

subtopic: A power cut or rain spoils plans
subtype: Approach: making a back-up plan for outdoor events [Thinking]
passage: Monday. Aditi's birthday was planned for the garden on Saturday. Her friend Imran pushed his glasses up and said the clouds looked heavy. "Then we need a Plan B," Aditi said. "If it rains we move to the hall behind the flats. Two sets of games: cards and skipping ropes for outside, board games and pass-the-parcel for inside." She packed two boxes. Saturday. Rain began at three. Everyone carried cake, chairs and the inside box into the hall within five minutes. Sunday. Imran said, "That was the best birthday I have been to, even with the rain." Aditi grinned and put both boxes back on the shelf, ready for next time.

qa.q: What did Aditi pack in the two boxes?
qa.a: She packed cards and skipping ropes for outside, and board games and pass-the-parcel for inside.

qa.q: What was Aditi feeling when Imran said the clouds looked heavy?
qa.a: A little worried that rain might spoil the party, but ready, since she made a Plan B on the spot.

qa.q: What else could Aditi add to her plan for the birthday?
qa.a: She could tell the guests about the hall option in advance, so everyone knows where to go if the weather changes.

qa.q: How did Imran see the birthday when the rain came?
qa.a: As the best birthday he had been to, because the move was quick and the party carried on.

grounding: A girl planning a garden birthday makes a rain plan with the hall and keeps games ready for both places.

subtopic: A power cut or rain spoils plans
subtype: Approach: finishing homework before the battery dies [Action]
passage: The storm warning crackled from the radio. "Ma, a storm is coming tonight," Sameer said, pulling the laptop closer. "So?" said his mother Sudha, stirring the dal. "So the online maths task is due tomorrow, and if the power goes, I lose it. I am doing it now." Forty minutes later he clicked Submit. "Done. Now I need the printer." "For what?" "The science notes. If there is no charge tomorrow, I still have paper." Sudha raised an eyebrow. "Since when do you plan like this?" Sameer grinned. "Since last time." At nine the lights went out. Warm under a blanket, Sameer read the printed pages by torchlight.

qa.q: What did Sameer print before the storm?
qa.a: He printed the science notes.

qa.q: Why did Sameer decide to finish the online task early, and what was he worried about?
qa.a: He worried that a power cut would make him miss the deadline, so he wanted the task safely submitted.

qa.q: What other step could Sameer take against an outage, and why?
qa.a: He could charge the phone and laptop fully and keep a torch nearby, because he can keep working or reading if the lights go.

qa.q: How might Sudha feel seeing Sameer plan this well?
qa.a: Surprised and pleased, since she raised an eyebrow and asked since when he plans like this. 🙂

grounding: A boy finishes an online task early and prints notes before a storm, so a power cut cannot strand him.

subtopic: A power cut or rain spoils plans
subtype: Approach: safety thinking during a storm [Thinking]
passage: Thunder cracked over the flat, and Mummy was still stuck at the bus stop, so Sabina was in charge of her little brother Aman for the next half hour. Her heart thumped, but she remembered Gopika Ma'am's lesson word for word. Keep away from wet switches. Keep away from wires and windows. Unplug the television. She pulled the television plug with a dry hand, called Aman away from the balcony door, and sat with him on the mattress in the middle room, well away from the window. Then she rang Mummy to say all was fine. "Well done," Mummy said, her voice shaky with relief. "Stay right there. I am nearly home."

qa.q: Which safety actions did Sabina take during the storm?
qa.a: She unplugged the television, called Aman away from the balcony door and sat with him in the middle room, away from the window.

qa.q: What was Sabina feeling when the thunder cracked and Mummy was not home?
qa.a: Frightened, since her heart thumped, but she steadied herself by recalling the rules from school. 😰

qa.q: What else could Sabina do if the storm got worse?
qa.a: Stay in the middle room and keep the phone close to call Mummy or a trusted adult nearby, because a grown-up can help if something goes wrong.

qa.q: How might Mummy feel while stuck at the bus stop?
qa.a: Anxious about the children, which is why her voice was shaky with relief when Sabina said all was fine.

grounding: A girl remembers school storm rules and follows them: no wet switches, unplug the television, stay away from windows.

subtopic: A power cut or rain spoils plans
subtype: Approach: turning the problem into a game [Revision]
passage: Two hours into the power cut Leela had sighed thirty times, and Deepak had kicked the sofa twice. Rain drummed on the window, so going out was no use. "This is the worst evening," Deepak said. Then the torch beam slid across the wall and Leela's fingers moved without thinking. A rabbit. "Deepak, look." He frowned, then made a dog with his hand, and the dog chased the rabbit. A crocodile joined, then a giant bird, and they invented a story about a rabbit crossing a river with mangoes for a sleeping king. Amma looked in from the kitchen and stayed, holding her tea, to watch the crocodile. When the lights returned, both groaned. "Switch it off," said Deepak. "We are not finished."

qa.q: What animal did Leela make first with her hands in the torch beam?
qa.a: Leela made a rabbit first.

qa.q: What was Deepak feeling at the start of the evening?
qa.a: Bored and cross, as shown when he kicked the sofa and called it the worst evening.

qa.q: What other approach could the siblings try if the power cut lasted even longer?
qa.a: They could play a guessing game or sing, because those also need no electricity and keep them busy together. 😊

qa.q: How might Amma see the siblings' game after such a restless start?
qa.a: With relief and warmth, since she stayed in the doorway with her tea to watch instead of leaving.

grounding: Two siblings turn a dull evening without electricity into shadow puppets and a made-up story.

subtopic: A power cut or rain spoils plans
subtype: Approach: waiting passively for things to return to normal [Pitfall]
passage: Urmila, stop sighing at the ceiling and listen. I am Anand, and when I was a boy of nine the lights went out across our lane for a whole evening. I sat on the sofa with my arms folded and said "I am bored" every few minutes. Nothing more. My sister was drawing by candle light, my cousin was drumming a rhythm on an upturned bucket, and Nani was telling stories, and I sat there like a stone, waiting for the fan to turn again. Three hours, Urmila, and I did none of it. When the lights came on I was more tired than if I had run around. And nobody had stopped me joining in.

qa.q: What did Anand say every few minutes during the power cut?
qa.a: Anand said "I am bored".

qa.q: How was Anand feeling while sitting on the sofa with folded arms?
qa.a: Bored and cross, since Anand complained again and again and waited for the fan to turn.

qa.q: What could Anand have tried instead of waiting, and why?
qa.a: Anand could have joined the drawing or the drumming on the bucket, because the family activities were right there.

qa.q: How might Anand's sister and cousin have seen Anand sitting there?
qa.a: They may have wondered why Anand did not join, since they were busy having fun and nobody had stopped Anand.

grounding: A child sits doing nothing until the lights return, bored and complaining, though many activities were available.
